sections.overview: Acasis viretata is a small geometrid moth found across much of Europe and eastward into Asia. It is named for the yellow-green and dark cross-lines of its forewings, but fresh adults are greener than older specimens because the colour fades quickly. Its caterpillars feed on flowers, fruits and leaves of several shrubs and climbing plants, including holly, ivy and privet.
sections.identification: The adult has a compact, finely patterned outline with olive or yellow-green forewings crossed by dark, wavy lines; small black dots often interrupt the pale outer band. Fresh moths can be vivid green, but the ground colour fades to yellowish or grey-brown, so colour alone is unreliable. The hindwings are pale grey. The wingspan is 25–29 mm; sources give no meaningful body height, width or mass, and no consistent male–female size difference. Compare the full cross-line pattern and hindwing with other small Larentiinae rather than relying on the faded colour.
sections.habitat: It occurs in deciduous woodland, scrub, hedgerows, parks and gardens where its caterpillar foodplants grow. French records also place it in open woodland, damp clearings and some mountain areas. Across Europe the species is widespread but often local or encountered sparingly; local status differs considerably between regions.
sections.diet: The caterpillars feed on several plant genera rather than one exclusive host. Regional moth records list holly (Ilex), ivy (Hedera), privet (Ligustrum), dogwood (Cornus), guelder-rose (Viburnum) and buckthorn (Rhamnus); larvae may eat flowers, developing fruits and leaves. Adults do not feed on these plants in the same way, and no species-specific adult nectar preference was found in the sources reviewed.
sections.behavior: Adults fly mainly in spring and summer, with a second generation in the southern part of the range in some years or regions. They are often found singly at light and may rest on tree trunks during the day. The green colour is most evident just after emergence and fades with age, which can make older specimens appear like a different moth.
sections.reproduction: The female lays eggs on or near suitable foodplants. Caterpillars are recorded in early summer and feed on flowers, fruits and foliage; the species overwinters as a pupa. Depending on latitude and local conditions, it may have one or two adult flight periods. Detailed, species-wide figures for egg number, development time and sex-specific size were not found.
sections.ecology: Its larvae use a range of common shrubs and climbers, while adults are part of the nocturnal moth community of woodland edges and gardens. The pupa passes the winter, linking the life cycle to seasonal plant growth. Regional records suggest it can be widespread without being abundant at any one site; no quantitative ecological role or population trend was established in the references reviewed.
sections.conservation: The reviewed sources do not indicate a global threat assessment specific to Acasis viretata. It is widespread across a broad range, though local records may be sparse and regional status varies. Maintaining structurally varied woodland edges, hedgerows and host plants supports the habitat used by its larvae, but this is a general habitat measure rather than evidence of a species-specific decline.
